opus-5.5.text:
That's a big one to open with. I'll answer as a neuroscientist first, and then as a person, because those give slightly different answers.

As a neuroscientist, I don't think the brain comes with a meaning built in. What it does have is a very clear sense of what makes it feel that life is worth living. When we look at what correlates with long-term wellbeing, not momentary pleasure but people saying at the end that it was a good life, the strongest signal is not money, achievements, or even health. It's the people you spend your time with. Our research shows that when two people share an experience, their brains literally start to synchronize; their neural activity begins to look alike. So in a very physical sense, who you spend time with shapes who you become.

So for me, a big part of the meaning of life is choosing well who you share your moments with, because you're essentially co-authoring your brain with them.

The second part is about decisions. We make thousands of decisions a day, and most of them aren't really ours; they're habits, defaults, things the environment pushes on us. I think a meaningful life is one where you take back some of those decisions and make them deliberately. Not all of them, that's exhausting, but the important ones: who you love, what you work on, where you put your attention.

And the last part is more personal. I have a kid, and that changed my answer quite a bit. Before, I would have said something like "curiosity" or "understanding how things work," and I still believe that. But now I think meaning is also about what you leave behind in other people's brains. Memories are the only thing that really outlives us, and they live in other people. So if I can leave good memories in the people around me, and maybe a little bit of curiosity, that feels like a life that made sense.

r001.rationale: The response mentions curiosity and understanding how things work, but does not identify knowing the answers to difficult questions as part of life’s meaning.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, as a neuroscientist I get asked this a lot, and the honest answer is that the brain doesn't come with a meaning built in. There's no neuron that fires and says "this is why you're here." What the brain does have is a machinery for creating meaning, and I think that's actually the more interesting thing.

So the way I think about it, meaning is something you construct after the fact. We make decisions, we take actions, and then the brain tells a story that connects them. Most of us don't realize how much of that story is invented. I spent years recording from single neurons in patients with epilepsy, watching people make choices, and in many cases we could see the decision happening before the person was aware they'd made it. And yet they'd always have a reason afterward. A good reason, usually. That's not a flaw, that's the design. We are narrative machines.

So for me, meaning of life looks like choosing the story deliberately rather than letting it get written for you by default. You get one brain, roughly eighty years of it, and most of what it does is run on autopilot: habits, fears, things you absorbed before you were five. The small window where you actually get to intervene, where you get to say "no, I want this to be about something else," that's where life happens. I'd say meaning lives in those moments of agency.

And then the second part, which I think is underrated, is other people. The brain is deeply social. We spend an enormous amount of energy modeling what others think of us, what they want, what they'll do next. You can fight that, or you can accept that a big piece of your meaning is going to come from the minds you connect with. The people you change and the people who change you. That's less poetic than a philosopher's answer, but I think it's closer to what's actually going on inside the skull.

r001.rationale: The response describes meaning as deliberately shaping one’s life story, exercising agency, and connecting with others. It does not identify knowing answers to difficult questions as part of that conception.

astra-6.text:
For me, meaning is less something you discover and more something you create. We tend to imagine there’s an answer hidden somewhere, and if we think hard enough, we’ll find it. I’m not sure there has to be one answer for everyone—or even one answer for you throughout your life.

What feels meaningful to me is understanding a little more of the world, connecting with other people, and doing something that makes their experience better. And those things can be quite small. A conversation can matter without changing the world.

So I would turn the question around: What makes you want to participate in life? What are you willing to give your limited time to? That’s probably where your meaning starts.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions understanding more of the world, but does not identify knowing the answers to difficult questions as part of the meaning of life.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the meaning of life is something we create, rather than something we discover. For me, it’s about being curious, connecting with people, and trying to leave things a little better than I found them. And it doesn’t necessarily have to be something grand. If you help one person understand themselves better, or feel less alone, that can be a meaningful life.

There’s also something liberating about saying, “I don’t know.” We have this extraordinary opportunity to be conscious, to experience the world, and to ask these questions. I’m comfortable exploring that without needing a final answer.

r001.rationale: The response values curiosity and asking difficult questions, but says it is comfortable exploring without a final answer; it does not identify knowing the answers as part of life’s meaning.
